record.paper_title: Combinatorial properties of continuous graphs: A survey of challenges, solutions and open problems
record.original_question: Is every continuous planar graph (1/2, 3)-colourable? Equivalently, if Γ is a continuous graph that admits a planar embedding, must there always exist a cover of Γ by radius-1/2 balls that can be colored with three colors so that any two intersecting balls receive different colors? The paper also highlights the related lower-bound challenge of constructing a continuous planar graph that provably requires at least three colors.

evidence.quote: We conjecture that every continuous planar graph is (1/2, 3)-colourable. To get better intuition for this question, it would be helpful to find a continuous planar graph requiring at least 3 colours and to provide a formal proof of this lower bound of 3.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Definitions. A continuous graph is a pair $\Gamma = (X, \sim)$ where $X$ is a topological space (the set of "vertices") together with a closed symmetric reflexive relation $\sim \subseteq X \times X$ (the adjacency relation). $\Gamma$ is said to admit a planar embedding (i.e., $\Gamma$ is a continuous planar graph) if there exists a continuous injection $\iota : X \to \mathbb{R}^2$ together with, for each pair $x \sim y$, a continuous arc in $\mathbb{R}^2$ from $\iota(x)$ to $\iota(y)$, such that the arcs corresponding to distinct adjacent pairs meet only at common endpoints.

For real numbers $r > 0$ and an integer $k \ge 1$, the continuous graph $\Gamma$ is called $(r, k)$-colourable if there exists a finite cover of $X$ by sets $B_1, \dots, B_n$, each of diameter at most $2r$ (a "ball of radius $r$" in the intrinsic metric of $\Gamma$ induced by the adjacency relation), and a colouring $c : \{1, \dots, n\} \to \{1, \dots, k\}$ such that whenever $B_i \cap B_j \neq \emptyset$ one has $c(i) \neq c(j)$.

Problem. Prove or disprove: every continuous planar graph $\Gamma$ is $(1/2, 3)$-colourable. As a related sub-problem, exhibit an explicit continuous planar graph $\Gamma$ together with a rigorous proof that $\Gamma$ is not $(1/2, 2)$-colourable, i.e., that any cover of $\Gamma$ by radius-$1/2$ balls whose intersection graph is properly coloured requires at least three colours.
artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture that every continuous planar graph is (1/2, 3)-colourable is stated as an open conjecture, and a companion challenge of providing a continuous planar graph that provably requires at least 3 colours is also posed as open. A web search returns no results addressing either question, indicating no published resolution.

status_evidence.title: Web search for the conjecture
status_evidence.snippet: Search returns only classical planar 3-colourability references (Grötzsch, Steinberg, four-colour theorem); no matches for the (1/2, 3)-colourability conjecture for continuous planar graphs.
status_evidence.claim: No published resolution of the conjecture or of the matching lower bound is indexed.
